t: Minimum Unique Word Abbreviation — Bitmask Editorial
o: An abbreviation is fully determined by which positions of the target are kept as letters; the rest are merged into maximal runs replaced by their lengths. So we can represent any abbreviation by a bitmask over the $m$ positions of `target` (bit set = letter kept), and the abbreviation's length equals the number of kept letters plus the number of zero-runs. A dictionary word can only collide with the target if it has the same length $m$ (different-length words share no abbreviation). For a same-length word, the abbreviation given by `mask` also abbreviates that word exactly when the word agrees with the target on every position where `mask` keeps a letter — i.e. when `mask & diff(word) == 0`, where `diff` marks positions where they differ. In Example 1, mask `01111` gives "a4", which does not match "blade" because position 0 differs; mask `11110` gives "4e" which matches "blade"'s last letter 'e', so it is invalid. The constraint $\log_2(n)+m \le 21$ hints that $n$ is small relative to $2^m$, making bitmask enumeration/search viable.
k: Every abbreviation corresponds one-to-one to a subset (bitmask) of kept positions; length = popcount + number of zero-runs.
Only dictionary words with length equal to len(target) can ever conflict.
A mask conflicts with a word iff mask & diff(word) == 0, where diff marks mismatched positions; we need the minimum-popcount mask hitting every diff.
The guarantee log2(n) + m <= 21 means the number of relevant words is tiny compared to 2^m, enabling targeted search.

a.i: Enumerate all $2^m$ subsets of kept positions, render each into an abbreviation string, and check whether it is an abbreviation of any same-length dictionary word (a word w is abbreviated by mask only if w[i] == target[i] at every kept position i). Track the shortest valid abbreviation. With $m \le 21$ this is about 2M masks times a cheap check per word — fast enough.
s: Filter dictionary to words of length m; for each, precompute nothing yet.
For each mask in [0, 2^m): render the abbreviation string of target (kept letters, merged runs of zeros as lengths).
For each filtered word, verify that at every kept bit position the word's character equals target's character; if some word passes, the mask is invalid.
Among valid masks keep the one with minimal abbreviation length (popcount + zero-runs); return its string.
a.t: O(2^m · n · m) — for each of 2^m masks we scan up to n words of length m.
a.sp: O(n·m) for the filtered word list plus O(m) rendering buffers.

a.n: Approach 2: Conflict-driven backtracking on diff masks
a.i: Precompute, for each same-length word, a diff bitmask of positions where it differs from the target. Mask M is invalid iff M & diff == 0 for some word. Instead of scanning all 2^m masks, do a DFS: pick any currently-unsatisfied word (one whose diff has empty intersection with the current mask) and branch on setting one of its diff bits — every completion must include at least one such bit. Prune branches whose popcount already reaches the best found. Since log2(n) + m <= 21, few words exist and the search tree stays small.
s: Filter dictionary to length-m words and compute diff[word] = OR of (1<<i) where word[i] != target[i].
DFS with current mask: find the first word with mask & diff == 0; if none exists, record this mask as a candidate (update best by popcount) and return.
Otherwise, for each set bit b in that word's diff, recurse with mask | (1<<b).
Prune recursion when popcount(mask) >= popcount(best) (or when no better solution than current best+1 is possible).
Render the best mask into its abbreviation string and return it.
a.t: O(n·m + k·m) where k is the number of masks visited by the pruned DFS — far below 2^m in practice thanks to branching only on necessary conflict bits and the small-n constraint.
a.sp: O(n + m) for diff masks and recursion depth at most m.

w: In an interview, start with Approach 1 to establish correctness, then present Approach 2 as the optimization: the key reframing is that validity depends only on which positions are kept, and conflicts reduce to bitwise intersections with per-word diff masks. Pitfalls: forgetting to filter out words whose length differs from the target (they can never collide); miscounting abbreviation length (it is letters kept plus number of zero-runs, not just popcount); handling the empty dictionary (answer is simply the full-number abbreviation "m"); and off-by-one when merging runs. Edge cases: single-character target, dictionary containing words longer than target, and ties in length (any answer accepted). Follow-ups might ask for the lexicographically smallest shortest abbreviation, or scaling m beyond 21, which would require meet-in-the-middle or ILP-style techniques.
